title: GitOps & Infrastructure as Code
scopeHtml:
Scope: GitOps and pull-based deployment, Argo CD, Terraform and state, secrets in Git, policy as code and drift.

Scope: Helm vs Kustomize, promotion, CI-to-GitOps handoff, Terraform in depth, cloud networking and IAM, config management and FinOps.

notes.title: GitOps: Git as the source of truth
notes.html:
GitOps means the desired state of your infrastructure and applications lives in a Git repository, and an automated agent inside the cluster continuously makes the cluster match Git. To deploy you do not run kubectl apply from a laptop or a CI job; you open a PR that changes a manifest, and after merge the agent pulls and applies it.

Principles: declarative config, versioned and immutable history in Git, automatically pulled, continuously reconciled (drift is corrected).

Push (classic CI deploy): CI holds cluster credentials and runs kubectl/helm. Pull (GitOps): the agent in the cluster pulls from Git; CI never needs production credentials.

Worked example. Someone manually edits a Deployment to 10 replicas during an incident and forgets. With Argo CD self-heal on, it reverts to the Git value (3) within minutes, or alerts about drift; rollback of a bad release is git revert.

Industry examples. Intuit created Argo CD; Flux (Weaveworks, now CNCF) is the other major tool. Adopted at Adobe, Ticketmaster, Tesla and many banks for audit trails.

Everyday analogy. A thermostat: you set the target temperature once; the system keeps adjusting to match, and someone opening a window gets corrected.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying GitOps = "CI/CD tool". It specifically means pull-based reconciliation from Git, with Git as the only way to change prod.
  • Mixing app code and environment config in one repo without thinking about access and noise.

notes.title: Argo CD in practice
notes.html:
An Argo CD Application points at a Git path (Helm chart/Kustomize/plain YAML) and a destination cluster and namespace. It compares live state with Git, shows OutOfSync, and syncs manually or automatically.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata: { name: api-prod, namespace: argocd }
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/deploy-config
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/api/overlays/prod
  destination: { server: https://kubernetes.default.svc, namespace: api }
  syncPolicy:
    automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }   # delete removed resources, undo manual drift
    syncOptions: [CreateNamespace=true]

Common layout: an app repo (code, Dockerfile, CI) and a separate config repo (manifests per environment). CI builds the image, then opens a PR or commits to the config repo bumping the tag (Argo CD Image Updater or a scripted step automates this). ApplicationSets generate many Applications (per cluster or per team).

Industry examples. Platform teams manage hundreds of services with one ApplicationSet; promotion dev → staging → prod is a PR moving the same image tag between overlay folders.

Everyday analogy. A blueprint board in the site office: workers only build what's on the approved drawing, and an inspector flags anything that differs.

Common interview traps.

  • prune: true without understanding it deletes resources removed from Git (including by accident).
  • Storing plain Secrets in the config repo (use Sealed Secrets, SOPS or External Secrets).

notes.title: Infrastructure as Code and Terraform
notes.html:
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) defines servers, networks, databases and permissions in files, reviewed and versioned like code, instead of clicking in a cloud console. Benefits: repeatable environments, review, audit, disaster recovery by re-applying.

Terraform (and OpenTofu) is declarative and cloud-agnostic. Workflow: terraform init → plan (shows what will change) → apply. It keeps a state file mapping your code to real resources, which must be stored remotely with locking (S3 + DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud) and never committed; state may contain secrets.

terraform {
  backend "s3" { bucket = "acme-tf-state" key = "prod/network.tfstate" region = "ap-south-1"
                 dynamodb_table = "tf-locks" encrypt = true }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" {
  bucket = "acme-prod-logs"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "logs" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.logs.id
  versioning_configuration { status = "Enabled" }
}

CI runs plan on every PR and posts the diff; apply runs after merge with approval. Modules package reusable pieces (a VPC, a service).

Other tools: Pulumi (real languages), AWS CloudFormation/CDK, Ansible (configuration management, procedural/idempotent), Crossplane (Kubernetes-native IaC).

Worked example. Rebuilding a staging environment manually takes a day and differs each time; terraform apply creates the same 80 resources in ~15 minutes.

Industry examples. HashiCorp Terraform is the de facto multi-cloud choice; many teams run Atlantis to plan/apply from PR comments.

Everyday analogy. A building plan the contractor can rebuild from anywhere, rather than a house built by memory.

Common interview traps.

  • Two engineers applying at the same time without state locking corrupt state.
  • Changing resources by hand in the console (drift), so next apply surprises everyone.
  • terraform destroy or an immutable-field change (force replacement) on a database: always read the plan.

notes.title: Environments, config and secrets
notes.html:
Keep per-environment differences small and explicit: Kustomize overlays or Helm values per environment, Terraform workspaces or separate state per environment. Production should be a copy of staging with different sizes and credentials, not a different design.

Secrets do not belong as plain text in Git. Options:

  • Sealed Secrets: encrypt with a cluster key; only the cluster can decrypt; encrypted file is safe in Git.
  • SOPS (with KMS/age): encrypts values in YAML in place.
  • External Secrets Operator / CSI driver with Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or GCP Secret Manager: Git stores a reference only.

Also rotate secrets regularly and use workload identity (IAM role per service account) instead of static keys.

Industry examples. Banks and fintechs commonly use Vault plus dynamic short-lived database credentials.

Everyday analogy. The recipe is public in the cookbook (Git); the safe-combination is kept in a separate locked box (secret store) and the cookbook just says "see safe".

Common interview traps.

  • Base64-encoded secrets committed to Git.
  • Different configuration structure in each environment, so staging proves nothing about prod.

notes.title: Policy as code and drift
notes.html:
Guardrails run automatically in PRs and in the cluster: OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno policies ("no image from unknown registries", "no root containers", "every pod has resource limits"), Conftest/tfsec/Checkov for Terraform. These stop risky config before it merges.

Drift is the difference between declared and real state, caused by manual changes. Detect it (terraform plan on a schedule, Argo CD OutOfSync alerts) and decide: revert or codify.

Worked example. A policy blocks any Service of type LoadBalancer without an approved annotation, preventing an accidental public database endpoint.

Industry examples. Capital One-style cloud governance and many regulated teams enforce policy as code for compliance evidence.

Everyday analogy. Building code inspectors who check plans before construction starts.

Common interview traps.

  • Enforcing policies only at deploy time; shift them left into the PR as well.

notes.title: Helm vs Kustomize
notes.html:
Both manage per-environment variations of Kubernetes YAML.

  • Helm packages manifests as a templated chart with values.yaml. It tracks releases (history, helm rollback), supports hooks and dependencies, and has a large public chart ecosystem. Downsides: Go-template YAML is hard to read and debug.
  • Kustomize (built into kubectl) keeps plain YAML and applies patches/overlays (base/ plus overlays/prod). No templating language; less flexible for heavy parameterisation.
apps/api/
  base/            deployment.yaml service.yaml kustomization.yaml
  overlays/dev/    kustomization.yaml   (replicas: 1)
  overlays/prod/   kustomization.yaml   (replicas: 6, higher limits, image tag)

Common pattern: use Helm for third-party software (ingress controller, Prometheus) and Kustomize or Helm for your own services; Argo CD supports both.

Industry examples. Most teams install community charts for infrastructure and keep their own apps as Helm charts with a shared "library chart" for standards.

Everyday analogy. Helm is a fill-in-the-blanks form letter; Kustomize is the original letter with sticky notes saying "change this line for the Mumbai office".

Common interview traps.

  • Helm values files that contain real secrets.
  • Overusing template logic until nobody can read the chart.

notes.title: Multi-environment promotion
notes.html:
Promote the same image digest dev → staging → prod. In GitOps this is changing the tag in the next environment's folder or values file through a PR (or automated after checks pass). Environments should be as similar as possible: same manifests, differing only in size, endpoints and secrets.

Structure options: a folder per environment on one branch (preferred, easy diffs and reviews) rather than a branch per environment (merge drift, confusing).

Automate the dev bump, require tests plus an approval for prod, and keep an audit log in Git.

Industry examples. Kargo (for Argo CD), Flux image automation and Spinnaker pipelines implement promotion; many shops script it with a bot opening PRs.

Everyday analogy. A product passing quality checkpoints on an assembly line, each signed off before the next.

Common interview traps.

  • A branch per environment leading to config drift.
  • Staging smaller or different enough that it proves nothing about prod.

notes.title: From CI to GitOps: the handoff
notes.html:
The CI/CD split: CI builds, tests, scans and pushes an immutable image. CD (GitOps) deploys it. The handoff is a commit to the config repo changing the image reference.

Ways to do it: a CI step that edits the manifest and opens a PR or pushes to a bot-owned branch; Argo CD Image Updater or Flux image automation watching the registry; or a promotion tool (Kargo). Ensure the commit message links the source commit and build for traceability.

# CI step (simplified)
yq -i '.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image = "ghcr.io/acme/api:'$GITHUB_SHA'"' deploy/prod/api.yaml
git commit -am "api: bump to $GITHUB_SHA" && git push

Worked example. Argo CD notices a new commit in deploy-config, shows OutOfSync, syncs, and reports health. If the new pods fail readiness, the sync is marked Degraded and an alert fires; the fix is a git revert.

Industry examples. Intuit, Adobe and many fintechs use this split with a separate config repo owned by the platform team.

Everyday analogy. The factory (CI) boxes the product and puts a label on the shelf order form; the store (CD) restocks based on that form.

Common interview traps.

  • CI that pushes straight to the cluster with admin credentials, defeating the pull model.
  • No link from deployed version back to the source commit.

notes.title: Terraform in depth: modules, environments and testing
notes.html:
Modules package reusable infrastructure (a VPC, an EKS cluster, a service) with inputs and outputs, versioned and pinned. For environments, prefer separate state and directories per environment (or per component) over a single giant state: smaller blast radius, faster plans. Workspaces exist but can hide which environment you are touching.

Useful practices: terraform fmt/validate and tflint in CI; plan on PR, apply on merge (Atlantis, Terraform Cloud, GitHub Actions); policy checks (OPA/Conftest, Sentinel); lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } on stateful resources; moved blocks for refactors; provider and module version pins with a lock file; terratest or terraform test for modules.

module "orders_db" {
  source  = "git::https://github.com/acme/tf-modules.git//rds?ref=v2.1.0"  # pinned
  name    = "orders"
  size    = "db.r6g.large"
  deletion_protection = true
}

Industry examples. Many companies keep an internal module registry owned by the platform team so every database comes with backups, encryption and alarms by default.

Everyday analogy. Prefabricated building modules with tested wiring that you assemble, instead of building each room from scratch.

Common interview traps.

  • One state file for the whole company.
  • Unpinned module versions that change underneath you.
  • Refactoring resource names without moved, causing destroy and recreate.

notes.title: Cloud networking and IAM basics for DevOps
notes.html:
Most pipeline and Kubernetes problems trace back to cloud fundamentals:

  • VPC with public and private subnets across multiple availability zones; databases and app servers in private subnets, NAT gateways for outbound access, a load balancer in public subnets.
  • Security groups (stateful, allow rules per resource) and network ACLs (stateless, per subnet).
  • Load balancers: L7 (ALB, HTTP routing) vs L4 (NLB, TCP, very high throughput).
  • IAM: users, roles, policies; apply least privilege; use roles and short-lived credentials, never long-lived keys; separate accounts for prod and non-prod.
  • DNS and CDN: Route 53/Cloud DNS, CloudFront/Cloudflare for caching and DDoS absorption.

Worked example. A pod cannot reach the internet to pull images: the node subnet is private and the NAT gateway route is missing. A security-group rule blocking port 443 outbound causes the same symptom.

Industry examples. AWS Well-Architected Framework and landing zones (Control Tower) standardise multi-account setups used by most enterprises.

Everyday analogy. A gated housing complex: public road (internet), reception (load balancer), residents' flats (private subnets), and key cards (IAM).

Common interview traps.

  • Databases in public subnets.
  • Wildcard IAM policies (*:*) "to get it working".

notes.title: Configuration management and FinOps basics
notes.html:
Configuration management (Ansible, Chef, Puppet) configures machines: installs packages, edits files, manages services. Ansible is agentless (SSH), procedural but aims for idempotence (running twice changes nothing the second time). In container-first setups, immutable infrastructure (bake an image, replace instances, never patch in place) reduces the need for it.

FinOps is cost management as an engineering practice: tag every resource with owner/team, track cost per service, right-size requests and instances, use autoscaling, spot/preemptible capacity for tolerant workloads, savings plans for steady load, delete idle environments (ephemeral PR environments with TTLs), and set budget alerts.

Worked example. Over-requested pods (4 CPU requested, 0.4 used) across 200 services waste about 60% of the cluster; right-sizing from VPA data cuts the bill by a third.

Industry examples. Cost visibility tools (Kubecost, OpenCost, cloud cost explorers) and spot-based autoscaling (Karpenter) are common in large organisations.

Everyday analogy. Switching off lights in empty rooms and buying the right size of car for your commute.

Common interview traps.

  • Mutating servers in place ("snowflakes") so nobody can recreate them.
  • Test environments left running over weekends with no owner tag.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: GitOps keeps desired state in Git and uses a pull-based agent (Argo CD, Flux) to reconcile the cluster, giving audit history, easy rollback by git revert and no production credentials in CI. Infrastructure as Code (Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation) makes cloud resources reproducible: plan in PR, apply after approval, store state remotely with locking. Keep environments structurally identical, handle secrets with Sealed Secrets, SOPS or external secret stores, and enforce guardrails with policy as code while watching for drift.

questions.promptHtml: What is GitOps and how does it differ from a traditional CI pipeline deploying with kubectl?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: GitOps is the dominant modern deployment model on Kubernetes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In GitOps the desired state lives in Git and an agent inside the cluster (Argo CD or Flux) continuously pulls it and reconciles the cluster to match. Traditional push CI holds cluster credentials and runs kubectl apply. GitOps removes production credentials from CI, gives a full audit history, corrects drift automatically, and rolls back with git revert.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A typical flow: CI builds and pushes an image, then updates the image tag in a config repo; Argo CD detects the change and syncs. Separate app repo and config repo keeps deployment changes auditable and reviewable. Self-heal reverts manual changes.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling any CD tool "GitOps". Pull-based reconciliation from Git is the defining feature.
  • Plain secrets in the config repo.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Downside? → Extra repo and tooling, eventual consistency, learning curve.
  2. How do you promote between environments? → A PR changing the tag or overlay for the next environment.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior discusses repo layout, promotion flow and access control.

questions.promptHtml: What do automated, prune and selfHeal do in an Argo CD sync policy?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests hands-on understanding and risk awareness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: automated syncs when Git changes without a manual click. prune deletes cluster resources that were removed from Git. selfHeal reverts manual changes made directly in the cluster so it always matches Git.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: These make Git authoritative but add danger: prune can delete something removed by mistake, so use PR review and protect critical resources with sync options or annotations. Without selfHeal, drift persists until the next sync. ApplicationSets generate many Applications for multi-cluster or multi-team setups.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Enabling prune on a namespace containing resources Argo does not own.
  • Hotfixing with kubectl in an incident and being surprised when it reverts.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you do an emergency hotfix? → Fast-path PR; or temporarily disable self-heal with a documented process.
  2. Where do secrets go? → External Secrets, Sealed Secrets or SOPS.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs the break-glass process and RBAC.

questions.promptHtml: What is Terraform state, and why must it be stored remotely with locking?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: State mishandling is a classic cause of IaC incidents.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: State maps the resources in your code to real cloud resources and records their attributes. It must be remote (for example S3 with DynamoDB locking, or Terraform Cloud) so the team shares one truth and a lock stops two people applying simultaneously and corrupting it. It can contain secrets, so encrypt it and restrict access.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Workflow is init, plan, apply; plans run in PRs, applies after approval. Split state by environment and component to limit blast radius and speed plans. Modules provide reuse. Drift happens when someone changes resources in the console; plan reveals it.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• State committed to Git.
  • Ignoring plan output that shows a database being replaced.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to handle drift? → Import or revert; restrict console write access.
  2. Terraform vs Ansible? → Provisioning declaratively vs configuring machines.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions state layout, prevent_destroy, and policy checks on plans.

questions.promptHtml: How do you store secrets safely in a GitOps workflow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: GitOps puts everything in Git, so secrets need a plan.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Never plain text. Either commit encrypted secrets (Sealed Secrets, SOPS with KMS or age) that only the cluster can decrypt, or keep secrets in an external manager (Vault, AWS or GCP Secret Manager) and commit only a reference that the External Secrets Operator resolves at runtime.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: External references are generally preferred: rotation happens in one place and Git never holds secret material, even encrypted. Use workload identity so the cluster authenticates to the secret manager without static keys, and audit access.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Base64 in Git, which is just encoding.
  • Long-lived static cloud keys in cluster secrets.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A secret leaked to Git history? → Rotate immediately; scrubbing history is secondary.
  2. Rotation? → Automate with short-lived dynamic credentials where possible.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior considers rotation, audit, and blast radius.

questions.promptHtml: What is policy as code and where would you enforce it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Governance at scale needs automation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Policy as code expresses guardrails as machine-checked rules, for example "no root containers", "images only from our registry", "every pod has resource limits". Enforce them in the PR (Conftest, Checkov, tfsec), and at deploy time in the cluster (OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno admission control) so violating resources are rejected.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Shift left gives fast feedback in the PR; admission control is the safety net for anything that bypasses it. Start in audit mode to measure violations before enforcing. Provide exemptions with expiry and a clear owner.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Enforcing only at admission, so developers learn at deploy time.
  • Turning enforcement on without an audit phase and breaking teams.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is drift? → Real state differing from declared state.
  2. Who owns policies? → A platform or security team, with a review process.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior phases rollout and manages exceptions.

questions.contextHtml: During an apply for a "small tagging change", Terraform destroys and recreates a production RDS database because an immutable field was modified in the same change. The plan output was long and was approved without close reading. Automated backups exist; the last snapshot is 3 hours old.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do now, and how do you prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the engineer and re-runs apply.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the apply still running? Is deletion_protection on? Which snapshot and point-in-time options exist?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the run if possible, cancel the pipeline, restore from the latest snapshot or point-in-time recovery, and point the application at the restored instance.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Immutable attribute change forcing replacement; a rename of the resource address; missing lifecycle guard.
  4. How I'd verify: Read the plan for -/+ (replace) markers and "forces replacement" annotations.
  5. Root cause: A forced-replacement change was approved without being flagged and no guard rails existed.
  6. Fix: Restore the data, reconcile state with terraform import or state commands, communicate data-loss window.
  7. Prevention: lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } and deletion_protection on databases, policy checks that fail plans containing destroy of stateful resources, smaller plans, mandatory plan summaries in the PR, separate state per component.
  8. Trade-offs: prevent_destroy blocks legitimate replacements, which then need a deliberate, reviewed override.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can you recover to the second before? → Point-in-time recovery if enabled, otherwise the snapshot only.
  • Who approves production applies? → Two people for stateful resources.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added a policy that rejected any plan deleting a database; the check paid for itself within a month.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames individual, repeats apply.
  • Hire: restores from backup, adds protection.
  • Strong hire: policy checks, state hygiene and recovery objectives (RPO/RTO).

questions.promptHtml: Compare Helm and Kustomize. When would you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The two standard tools for per-environment manifests.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Helm packages manifests as templated charts with values and tracks releases with rollback; it suits third-party software and heavy parameterisation. Kustomize keeps plain YAML and applies overlays and patches per environment, with no templating language. A common split is Helm for community software, either tool for your own services; Argo CD supports both.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Helm's Go-template YAML can become unreadable; Kustomize is less flexible for complex parameterisation. Keep real secrets out of values files.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Secrets in Helm values committed to Git.
  • Over-templating until nobody can debug the chart.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Helm rollback? → helm rollback to a previous revision.
  2. Chart standards? → A library chart for shared defaults.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior chooses by complexity and team skill.

questions.promptHtml: How do you structure environments and promotion in GitOps, and why avoid a branch per environment?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common design question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use a folder or overlay per environment on one branch and promote the same image digest by a PR (or automation) changing the tag for the next environment after checks pass. A branch per environment drifts, produces confusing merges and makes diffs hard to review.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Automate dev bumps, require tests plus approval for prod, and keep an audit trail in Git. Environments should be as similar as possible, differing in size, endpoints and secrets. Tools like Kargo or Flux image automation can drive promotion.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Staging so different from prod it proves nothing.
  • A long-lived branch per environment.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Rollback? → Revert the commit that changed the tag.
  2. Who approves prod? → Code owners on the prod folder.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs automated promotion with gates and evidence.

questions.promptHtml: How does CI hand an image off to a GitOps deployment?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The seam between CI and CD is where traceability is often lost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CI builds, tests, scans and pushes an immutable image, then commits the new image reference to the config repo through a PR or bot commit, or an image-updater tool watches the registry and writes it. The GitOps controller then syncs the cluster. The commit should link back to the source commit and build.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: CI never holds production cluster credentials. If new pods fail readiness the sync shows Degraded and alerts; rollback is a git revert of the config commit.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• CI pushing straight to the cluster with admin credentials.
  • No link from the deployed version to the source commit.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a separate config repo? → Different access, audit and change noise.
  2. Image Updater risk? → Auto-deploys; pair with environment gates.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior preserves traceability and least privilege end to end.

questions.promptHtml: How would you structure Terraform for multiple environments and keep it safe?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real IaC experience shows in the structure.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Reusable, versioned modules; separate state and directory per environment and component to limit blast radius; remote state with locking; plan on PR and apply after approval; pinned provider and module versions; policy checks on plans; prevent_destroy on stateful resources; and moved blocks for refactors.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: One giant state is slow and dangerous. Workspaces can hide which environment you are touching. Test modules with terraform test or Terratest, and use tflint and Checkov in CI.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• One state file for everything.
  • Unpinned modules changing underneath you.
  • Renaming resources without moved, causing destroy and recreate.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you import existing resources? → terraform import or import blocks.
  2. How do you share outputs? → Remote state data sources or a parameter store.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs for blast radius and review.

questions.promptHtml: A pod in a private subnet cannot pull images from the internet. What do you check?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many cluster issues are cloud-network issues.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The route table for the private subnet (is there a route to a NAT gateway), the NAT gateway itself, security group and network ACL rules allowing outbound 443, DNS resolution, and registry permissions via IAM. Better still, use VPC endpoints or a private registry mirror to avoid internet egress.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Standard layout: public subnets for load balancers, private subnets for apps and databases across multiple AZs. Security groups are stateful and attach to resources; NACLs are stateless per subnet. IAM should use roles with short-lived credentials.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Databases in public subnets.
  • Wildcard IAM policies "to get it working".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Security group vs NACL? → Stateful per resource vs stateless per subnet.
  2. How to lower NAT cost? → VPC endpoints for S3/ECR.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs network layout and endpoint usage for cost and security.

questions.contextHtml: The monthly cloud bill rose 45% in a quarter with no matching traffic growth. Kubernetes nodes run at ~25% average CPU utilisation, 40 preview environments from old PRs are still running, and no resources are tagged with an owner.
questions.promptHtml: How do you bring costs under control without hurting reliability?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Shrinks all nodes uniformly and removes headroom.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which services and accounts drive the bill? Peak-to-average ratios? Commitments already purchased?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Delete stale preview environments and add TTL cleanup; set budget alerts.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Over-requested pods; idle environments; oversized databases; data transfer or NAT costs; missing autoscaling.
  4. How I'd verify: Cost tools (Kubecost, OpenCost, cloud cost explorer) by tag, namespace and service; request versus usage graphs.
  5. Root cause: Requests set from guesses, no ownership tags, no cleanup of ephemeral resources.
  6. Fix: Right-size requests from VPA data, enable cluster autoscaling or Karpenter, use spot for tolerant workloads, savings plans for the steady base, tag enforcement.
  7. Prevention: Per-team cost dashboards, TTL on preview environments, policy requiring owner tags, monthly review.
  8. Trade-offs: Tighter sizing raises risk; keep headroom for peaks and use PDBs and autoscaling.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Teams resist cuts → show per-team cost and give them the data.
  • Spot interruptions → diversify instance types, handle SIGTERM and use PDBs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Right-sizing requests and removing idle environments cut a bill by about a third without a single incident.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: uniform cuts.
  • Hire: finds waste with data and right-sizes.
  • Strong hire: ownership, automation and risk-aware sizing.
